title: CGRC (2024 outline) practice exam

domains.name: Security and Privacy Governance, Risk Management, and Compliance Program
Selection and Approval of Framework, Security, and Privacy Controls
Implementation of Security and Privacy Controls
Assessment/Audit of Security and Privacy Controls

note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from ISC2's public CGRC exam outline (effective Jun 15, 2024). Not real exam questions. The real CGRC is 125 items in 3 hours, multiple choice and advanced item types.

q.q: In the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF), which step comes right BEFORE Select?
o: Categorize
Right. You categorize the system's impact level first, then select the baseline controls for that level.
Authorize
Authorize comes after Implement and Assess.
Monitor
Monitor is the last step, after authorization.
Assess
Assess checks controls that have already been selected and implemented.

q.q: Which RMF step was added in SP 800-37 Revision 2 to set up organization-wide roles, risk strategy and common controls before any one system is worked?
o: Prepare
Right. Prepare sets the context, roles and strategy at the organization and system levels.
Categorize
Categorize was already in Revision 1.
Decommission
Decommissioning isn't an RMF step.
Tailor
Tailoring is part of Select, not its own step.

q.q: What defines a system's authorization boundary?
o: What the AO accepts risk for
Right. Everything inside the boundary is covered by one authorization decision.
The building and floor where the servers are installed
A boundary is about components and management, not just a building.
Every system the company owns
That would be far too broad to assess and authorize as one.
The list of users who log in
Users matter, but the boundary is defined by components.

q.q: A control is partly provided by the cloud provider and partly configured by the agency's system team. What type of control is it?
o: A hybrid control
Right. Hybrid controls are part common (inherited) and part system-specific.
A common control
Common controls are fully provided by another source.
A compensating control
Compensating controls replace a control that can't be used.
A deterrent control
Deterrence is a control function, not where it comes from.

q.q: Which framework is mainly used to govern and manage enterprise IT, rather than to list security controls?
o: COBIT
Right. COBIT is an IT governance and management framework.
NIST SP 800-53
SP 800-53 is a catalog of security and privacy controls.
PCI DSS
PCI DSS sets security requirements for payment card data.
CIS Controls
The CIS Controls are a prioritized list of security safeguards.

q.q: During which phase of the system development life cycle should security and privacy requirements FIRST be defined?
o: Initiation
Right. Defining requirements early is far cheaper than adding them after the system is built.
Disposal
Disposal is the end of the life cycle.
Operations and maintenance
By then the design is set and changes cost more.
Implementation
Implementation builds what was already designed.

q.q: An organization's leadership says it will accept no more than a moderate risk to mission-critical systems. What has it defined?
o: Its risk tolerance
Right. Risk tolerance is the level of risk the organization is willing to accept.
Its risk register
The register lists specific risks.
Its control baseline
A baseline is a starting set of controls.
Its system boundary
A boundary defines a system's components.

q.q: Who formally accepts the risk of operating a federal information system?
o: The authorizing official (AO)
Right. The AO is a senior official who signs off on the risk to the organization.
The information system security officer (ISSO)
The ISSO handles day-to-day security for the system.
The control assessor
The assessor evaluates controls and reports findings.
The system administrator
Admins run the system but can't accept organizational risk.

q.q: Who is responsible for the system's day-to-day security operations, like keeping the SSP current and watching for changes?
o: The information system security officer (ISSO)
Right. The ISSO supports the system owner with daily security work.
The authorizing official
The AO makes the authorization decision, not daily operations.
The senior agency official for privacy
The SAOP oversees privacy across the organization.
An independent assessor
Assessors must stay separate from daily operations to stay independent.

q.q: Why should the control assessor be independent of the system team?
o: So the AO can trust the findings
Right. Independence keeps the assessment free from pressure or bias.
So the assessment takes less time
Independence isn't about speed.
So the assessor can change the controls
Assessors evaluate controls. They don't change them.
So the system team never sees the findings until after the ATO
The system team must see findings to fix them.

q.q: A data center team provides physical security controls that many systems inherit. What is this team called in the RMF?
o: A common control provider
Right. It's responsible for controls that many systems inherit.
An authorizing official
AOs accept risk. They don't provide the controls.
A system owner
Each system has its own owner. This team serves many systems.
A third-party assessor
Assessors evaluate controls. They don't provide them.

q.q: Which role is responsible for privacy risk across the whole organization, including approving privacy plans?
o: The senior agency official for privacy (SAOP)
Right. The SAOP oversees privacy policy and privacy risk.
The ISSO
The ISSO focuses on one system's security.
The help desk manager
The help desk doesn't own privacy risk.
The network engineer
Network engineers handle network configuration.

q.q: What is the MAIN purpose of a risk executive (function) in an organization?
o: To keep risk decisions consistent
Right. It gives an organization-wide view so each AO isn't deciding in isolation.
To run vulnerability scans on every system in the organization
Scanning is an operational task.
To replace the authorizing officials
AOs still make authorization decisions.
To write each system's security plan
System teams write their own plans.

q.q: A federal agency's information systems must follow which U.S. law that requires an agency-wide security program?
o: FISMA
Right. FISMA requires federal agencies to run security programs and authorize their systems.
HIPAA
HIPAA covers health information.
SOX
SOX covers public companies' financial reporting.
GLBA
GLBA covers financial institutions' customer data.

q.q: A cloud company wants to sell its SaaS product to U.S. federal agencies. Which program will it need to go through?
o: FedRAMP
Right. FedRAMP standardizes security authorization for cloud services used by federal agencies.
PCI DSS
PCI DSS covers payment cards.
ISO/IEC 27701
27701 is a privacy extension to ISO 27001, not federal authorization.
SOC 2 alone
A SOC 2 report helps, but it doesn't replace federal authorization.

q.q: A defense contractor handles Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). Which program checks that it protects that data?
o: CMMC
Right. CMMC assesses defense contractors' protection of federal contract information and CUI.
FedRAMP
FedRAMP covers cloud services for agencies.
HIPAA
HIPAA covers health data.
COPPA
COPPA covers children's data online.

q.q: A company processes personal data of EU residents. Which requirement means it may need to report a qualifying breach to regulators within 72 hours?
o: GDPR
Right. GDPR sets a 72-hour deadline to notify authorities of qualifying personal data breaches.
ISO/IEC 27001
ISO 27001 is a voluntary standard, not a law with deadlines.
NIST CSF
The CSF is voluntary guidance.
FISMA
FISMA applies to U.S. federal agencies.

q.q: An organization wants an internationally recognized certification of its information security management system. Which standard fits?
o: ISO/IEC 27001
Right. Organizations can be certified against ISO 27001's ISMS requirements.
NIST SP 800-53
SP 800-53 is a control catalog, not a certification.
FIPS 199
FIPS 199 is a categorization standard.
OWASP ASVS
ASVS is for application security verification.

q.q: Which document helps an organization decide whether a system's handling of personal data creates privacy risk that needs mitigation?
o: A privacy impact assessment (PIA)
Right. A PIA analyzes how personal data is collected, used and protected.
A penetration test report
A pentest finds technical weaknesses, not privacy impacts.
A load test plan
Load tests measure performance.
A business continuity plan
BCP keeps operations running.

q.q: A U.S. hospital adds a new patient portal. Which law's Security Rule sets safeguards for the electronic health information in it?
o: HIPAA
Right. HIPAA's Security Rule covers electronic protected health information.
FERPA
FERPA covers student records.
GDPR
GDPR is EU law and not the main U.S. health requirement.
CMMC
CMMC covers defense contractors.

q.q: Several frameworks require similar controls. Why do GRC teams build a control crosswalk?
o: To meet many requirements with one effort
Right. Mapping requirements together avoids doing the same work twice.
To remove the need for audits
Audits still happen. A crosswalk makes them easier.
To pick which law to ignore
All applicable laws must be met.
To rename controls so they match the newest framework's marketing
Crosswalks are about mapping, not branding.

q.q: Under the EU AI Act, which kind of AI system must meet requirements like risk management, documentation and human oversight before it can be used?
o: High-risk AI, like hiring tools
Right. High-risk systems carry duties like risk management, documentation and human oversight.
Every spam filter
Minimal-risk tools like spam filters face few or no new duties.
Only video games
Games are generally minimal risk.
Only AI systems that were built by companies outside the EU
It applies to AI placed on the EU market, wherever it was built.

q.q: Which document holds the system's name, purpose, boundary, environment and how each control is met?
o: The system security plan (SSP)
Right. The SSP describes the system and its controls in one place.
The plan of action and milestones (POA&M)
The POA&M tracks weaknesses and fixes.
The security assessment report (SAR)
The SAR records what the assessor found.
The incident response plan
The IR plan covers handling incidents.

q.q: Why must the system description list interconnections with other systems?
o: Data and risk can flow across those links
Right. Each connection can bring in risk and may need an agreement like an ISA.
So users know which printers to use
Printer choice isn't a reason to document interconnections.
Because interconnections are always outside the boundary and don't matter
They often sit at the boundary and matter a lot.
To increase the number of controls for the audit
The goal is to understand risk, not to pad the control count.

q.q: Two agencies connect their systems to share case data. Which document records the technical and security details of that link?
o: An interconnection security agreement (ISA)
Right. An ISA documents the connection's security requirements, often alongside an MOU.
A privacy notice
A privacy notice tells individuals how their data is used.
An acceptable use policy
An AUP covers how users may use systems.
A press release
A press release isn't a security document.

q.q: Which item is MOST important to include when describing the system's environment?
o: Where it runs and who manages each part
Right. The environment shows who is responsible for which controls.
The color of the server racks
Rack color has no security meaning.
The favorite tools and editors of the developers who built it
Tool preferences don't define the environment.
The size of the office break room
That isn't part of the system.

q.q: A system owner wants to include a vendor's SaaS app inside her system's authorization boundary. What should she check FIRST?
o: Whether her agency can oversee that service
Right. A boundary should include what the AO can actually hold accountable, often through the vendor's own authorization.
Whether the app has a modern interface that users will like
Branding doesn't affect the boundary.
Whether her team likes the app
Preference doesn't decide the boundary.
Whether the app is free
Price doesn't decide what's inside the boundary.

q.q: An inventory shows 40 servers, but the system description lists 32. What is the risk?
o: Eight servers may go unassessed
Right. Components missing from the description fall outside assessment and monitoring.
The description is too long
Length isn't the problem. Missing components are.
The servers will run faster
Documentation doesn't affect speed.
There is no risk, since servers are hardware and not software
Unknown hardware is a classic gap.

q.q: Which person is accountable for the system's overall development, operation and documentation, including the SSP?
o: The system owner
Right. The system owner is accountable for the system and its security documentation.
The authorizing official
The AO accepts risk but doesn't own the system.
The external auditor
Auditors evaluate. They don't own the system.
An end user
Users use the system. They don't own it.

q.q: A system stores two information types: public announcements (Low, Low, Low) and payroll data (Moderate, Moderate, Low). Under FIPS 199 and FIPS 200, what is the system's overall impact level?
o: Moderate
Right. The high-water mark takes the highest value across all information types.
Low
Payroll data pushes confidentiality and integrity to Moderate.
High
No information type reaches High.
It's averaged to Low-Moderate
FIPS 199 doesn't average. It uses the highest value.

q.q: A data loss would cause "severe or catastrophic" harm to the mission, assets or people. Which FIPS 199 impact level is this?
o: High
Right. High means severe or catastrophic adverse effects.
Moderate
Moderate means serious adverse effects.
Low
Low means limited adverse effects.
Not applicable
Every information type gets a rating.

q.q: Which NIST publication helps map information types to their recommended impact levels?
o: NIST SP 800-60
Right. SP 800-60 guides mapping information types to security categories.
NIST SP 800-88
SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
NIST SP 800-61
SP 800-61 covers incident handling.
NIST SP 800-63
SP 800-63 covers digital identity.

q.q: Why does the categorization decision matter so much later in the RMF?
o: It sets the starting control baseline
Right. Low, moderate and high systems get different baselines.
It decides the system's color on the network map and dashboards
Map colors aren't driven by categorization.
It sets the system's budget automatically
Budget is a separate decision.
It removes the need for an assessment
Every system still needs assessment.

q.q: A system will store data about EU customers and also process card payments. What should the team do while determining required compliance?
o: List every requirement that applies
Right. All requirements that apply must be identified before controls are chosen.
Pick the one framework it likes best
Every requirement that applies still has to be met.
Ignore GDPR because the company is based in the U.S.
GDPR can apply to non-EU companies handling EU residents' data.
Wait until the audit to find out
Finding out at audit time is too late and costly.

q.q: Who should review and approve the system's security categorization?
o: The AO or a designated representative
Right. Categorization drives everything after it, so senior approval matters.
Any developer on the team
Developers give input but don't approve.
The vendor that sold the software and supports it
The organization owns the decision.
The first user to log in
Users have no role in approval.

q.q: A system's information types are rated Moderate for confidentiality, High for integrity and Low for availability. What is its security category under FIPS 199?
o: {(confidentiality, MODERATE), (integrity, HIGH), (availability, LOW)}
Right. The security category lists each objective's value. The overall impact level for baselines would be High.
{(confidentiality, LOW), (integrity, LOW), (availability, LOW)}
That ignores the higher ratings.
Moderate, because that's the average
FIPS 199 doesn't average the values.
Not categorized, because the ratings differ
Different ratings are normal. Each objective is rated.

q.q: Which information about users belongs in the system description?
o: User types, roles and access paths
Right. User types and access paths shape access controls and risk.
Each user's home address and phone number for emergencies
Personal details aren't needed and create privacy risk.
Every user's password
Passwords must never be documented.
Users' favorite browsers
Browser preference isn't a security description.

q.q: A moderate-impact federal system is starting control selection. Where does the team begin?
o: The SP 800-53B moderate baseline
Right. Baselines give a starting set of controls for each impact level.
An empty list, adding controls as ideas come up
Starting from scratch risks missing required controls.
The high baseline, to be safe
Using the high baseline wastes effort and money on a moderate system.
Whatever controls the last project used
Another project's needs may be very different.

q.q: A system runs on a FedRAMP-authorized IaaS platform. How should the SSP treat the platform's physical and environmental controls?
o: Mark them as inherited from the provider
Right. Inherited controls are documented and relied on, not re-implemented.
Leave them out of the SSP completely
Inherited controls must still be documented.
Mark them as not applicable
They apply. They're just provided by someone else.
Re-test the provider's data center locks yourself
You rely on the provider's assessment rather than repeating it.

q.q: Why is it important to know which controls are inherited BEFORE implementation starts?
o: It avoids gaps and duplicate work
Right. Clear inheritance avoids gaps and duplicate work.
Inherited controls never fail
Common controls can fail too, which affects every system relying on them.
So the team can skip the SSP
The SSP is still required.
Inherited controls don't need any monitoring by anyone
They're monitored by the provider, and the system tracks their status.

q.q: A common control provider's assessment finds a weakness in a shared control. Who is affected?
o: Every system that inherits that control
Right. A weakness in a common control is a weakness for everyone relying on it.
Only the provider's own system
Inheriting systems share the weakness.
Nobody, because inherited controls are outside the boundary
Inherited controls protect systems inside their boundaries.
Only systems rated High
Any system inheriting the control is affected.

q.q: Which NIST publication lists the security and privacy controls that baselines are built from?
o: Right. SP 800-53 is the control catalog. SP 800-53B holds the baselines.
SP 800-30 is about conducting risk assessments.
SP 800-115 covers technical testing.
FIPS 140-3
FIPS 140-3 covers cryptographic modules.

q.q: What is the purpose of a privacy control baseline in SP 800-53B?
o: To start privacy control selection
Right. Privacy controls are selected based on privacy risk, separate from the security impact level.
To replace every security control
Privacy and security controls work together.
To decide which users get admin rights
That's access control, not the privacy baseline.
To categorize the system as low, moderate or high impact
Categorization is FIPS 199's job.

q.q: What is a security control overlay?
o: A tailored control set applied on a baseline
Right. Overlays adjust baselines for things like classified systems or industrial control systems.
A transparent sticker on a server
That's not a control concept.
A firewall rule that overrides every other rule in the policy
Overlays work at the control-selection level, not firewall rules.
A second copy of the SSP
Overlays modify control selection. They aren't copies of documents.

q.q: An agency uses an organization-wide awareness training program for all systems. How should each system's SSP list the awareness training control?
o: As a common control from the agency
Right. Organization-wide programs are common controls that systems inherit.
As system-specific, and each system builds its own training
That would be duplicated effort.
As not applicable
Training applies to every system's users.
As a compensating control
It isn't replacing anything.

q.q: When should the team document a control as "not applicable"?
o: When it truly doesn't fit, with a reason
Right. N/A needs a reason, such as no wireless means wireless controls don't apply.
When the control is hard or expensive to implement
Hard isn't the same as not applicable. Consider a compensating control.
When the team runs out of time
Deadlines don't change which controls apply.
Whenever a vendor says so
The organization decides and documents its own reasons.

q.q: Which document shows, for each control, whether it is system-specific, hybrid or inherited?
o: The system security plan
Right. The SSP records each control's implementation and source.
The incident report
Incident reports describe events.
The disaster recovery plan
The DR plan covers recovery.
The user manual
User manuals explain how to use the system.

q.q: A system has no wireless capability at all. During tailoring, what should happen to wireless controls?
o: Scope them out with a documented reason
Right. Scoping removes controls that can't apply, with the reasoning recorded.
Implement them anyway to pass the audit
Implementing controls for a feature that doesn't exist wastes effort.
Delete them without any note
Every tailoring decision needs to be documented.
Mark them as inherited
Nothing is providing them. They simply don't apply.

q.q: A baseline control requires account lockout after failed logins, but a 911 dispatch system can't lock out operators during an emergency. What is the BEST tailoring approach?
o: Use a compensating control, like alerts on repeated failures with a fast review, and document it
Right. Compensating controls reduce the risk when the baseline control would hurt the mission.
Drop the control and add nothing
Removing it without a substitute leaves the risk untreated.
Keep lockout, since the baseline requires it for every account
Locking out dispatchers in an emergency could cost lives.
Mark the control as inherited
Nothing is providing it.

q.q: Many SP 800-53 controls contain blanks like "[organization-defined frequency]." What should the team do with them?
o: Set values that fit the system's risk
Right. Organization-defined parameters let the control fit the environment.
Leave them blank so auditors choose
Auditors check against the values you set.
Always use the shortest possible value to be safe
The right value depends on risk, not on being shortest.
Copy values from a random website
Values should come from the organization's own analysis.

q.q: A threat assessment shows a moderate system faces advanced attackers. What should the team consider during selection?
o: Supplementing the baseline
Right. Baselines are a starting point. Higher threat can call for more.
Removing controls to keep the system simple
That raises risk when the threat is higher.
Changing the system to Low
Threat doesn't lower impact.
Waiting for an incident before adding any more controls
Waiting means taking avoidable risk.

q.q: Why should stakeholders agree to the selected controls before implementation?
o: To agree before money is spent
Right. Early agreement avoids rework and surprises at authorization.
Because stakeholders write the code
Stakeholders review. They don't usually build.
So the assessment can be skipped
Assessment is still needed.
Because the controls can't change later, even through change control
Controls can be adjusted later through change management.

q.q: During selection, the team also writes a plan for how controls will be checked over time. Which plan is this?
o: The continuous monitoring strategy
Right. Monitoring is planned during selection so it's built in from the start.
The marketing plan
Marketing isn't part of the RMF.
The hiring plan
Hiring isn't control monitoring.
The decommissioning plan
Decommissioning happens at end of life.

q.q: A system handles CUI, and the data must be marked and handled under specific rules. Where in selection are these rules addressed?
o: In tailoring, as handling rules
Right. Handling rules for sensitive data are part of tailoring the controls.
Only at decommissioning
Marking matters for the whole life of the data.
Never, since marking is optional for unclassified data
CUI marking rules are required.
Only after a breach
That's too late.

q.q: Which statement about tailoring is TRUE?
o: Tailoring decisions are recorded in the SSP
Right. Documented tailoring lets the AO and assessors see why the control set looks the way it does.
Tailoring only ever removes controls
Tailoring can also add or adjust controls.
Only auditors are allowed to tailor
The system team tailors, and the AO approves.
Tailored controls never need assessment by the independent assessor
Tailored controls are assessed like any other.

q.q: A hospital system needs extra controls for medical devices beyond the moderate baseline. A published, reusable set exists for this. What is that set called?
o: An overlay
Right. Overlays package extra or adjusted controls for a specific use case.
A POA&M
A POA&M tracks weaknesses.
A risk register
A register lists risks, not control sets.
An ATO
An ATO is an authorization decision.

q.q: A control enhancement in SP 800-53 is best described as what?
o: Added strength for a base control
Right. Enhancements build on a base control, like adding MFA requirements to identification and authentication.
A replacement for the base control in high systems
Enhancements add to the base control. They don't replace it.
An optional comment field
Enhancements are real control requirements when selected.
A vendor product feature
Enhancements are control requirements, not products.

q.q: Before implementing 200 controls, the team ranks them by risk, cost and dependencies and sets a timeline. What is it building?
o: An implementation strategy
Right. The strategy plans resources, funding, order and how effectiveness will be measured.
An incident response plan
IR plans cover handling incidents.
A decommissioning plan
That's for end of life.
A business impact analysis
A BIA ranks business processes for continuity.

q.q: How should the team decide which controls to implement FIRST?
o: The highest-risk ones and key dependencies
Right. Risk reduction and dependencies drive the order.
Alphabetically by control ID
IDs have nothing to do with risk.
Whatever is cheapest, regardless of risk, to show quick progress
Cheap but low-value controls can leave big risks open.
Whatever the newest team member prefers
Preference isn't a basis for priority.

q.q: How can the team show that a control is EFFECTIVE, not just installed?
o: Define effectiveness measures up front
Right. Measures show whether the control does its job.
Take a photo of the server
A photo doesn't show the control works.
Ask the vendor for a brochure
Brochures describe products, not your implementation.
Count how many pages the SSP has after implementation
Page count says nothing about effectiveness.

q.q: Implementing encryption on all databases needs new licenses and two months of work. Which part of the implementation strategy covers this?
o: Resourcing and funding
Right. The strategy must line up people, money and time for each control.
Categorization
Categorization happened earlier.
Decommissioning
That's at end of life.
Continuous monitoring
Monitoring comes after implementation.

q.q: Which item belongs in the implementation strategy for training-related controls?
o: Training frequency and tracking
Right. Training frequency and tracking are part of planning the control.
The trainer's favorite color
That isn't relevant.
A list of users' passwords
Never document passwords.
The date the system will be retired and replaced
Retirement isn't part of training planning.

q.q: Why classify each control as technical, administrative or physical during planning?
o: Each type needs different owners and evidence
Right. Knowing the type helps assign work and plan how to prove it.
Only technical controls are ever assessed, so the rest can be skipped
All control types are assessed.
Physical controls don't need owners
Every control needs an owner.
Administrative controls can't fail
Policies and procedures can fail too.

q.q: A key control depends on a new identity system that won't be ready for six months. What should the implementation strategy show?
o: The dependency and an interim measure
Right. Dependencies and interim steps keep the risk visible and managed.
Nothing, since it's out of the team's hands until the identity system ships
Hiding the gap leaves the AO uninformed.
That the control is fully in place already
That would be false documentation.
That the control is not applicable
It applies. It's just delayed.

q.q: Which stakeholder must usually agree when control implementation will cost more than budgeted?
o: The system owner
Right. The owner balances cost, schedule and risk for the system.
The external auditor who reviews the system each year
Auditors don't approve budgets.
Each end user
Users don't approve budgets.
The software vendor
The vendor doesn't control your budget.

q.q: The baseline requires multifactor authentication, but a legacy app can't support it. What should the team do?
o: Put a compensating control in place, like an MFA-protected gateway in front of the app, and document it
Right. Compensating controls reduce the risk when the standard control can't work.
Skip MFA and say nothing
That leaves the risk hidden and untreated.
Mark the control as implemented anyway, since MFA exists elsewhere
That's false documentation.
Turn off logins to the app
That stops the business.

q.q: Who should implement technical controls, like configuring audit logging on servers?
o: The assigned admins and engineers
Right. Implementation is done by the people who run the system, with clear assignments.
The independent assessor, since she knows the controls best
Assessors must stay independent of implementation.
The authorizing official
AOs make risk decisions. They don't configure servers.
The privacy officer
Privacy officers oversee privacy. They don't configure logging.

q.q: A team uses a hardened configuration standard like a DISA STIG or a CIS Benchmark when building servers. Which control area does this support?
o: Configuration management, through secure baseline settings
Right. Hardened baselines are how many configuration controls are met.
Physical security
Configuration standards are technical.
Privacy notices
These aren't privacy notices.
Contingency planning
Hardening isn't about recovery.

q.q: A privacy control says personal data must be collected only for stated purposes. How might the team implement it?
o: Collect only what the purpose needs
Right. Data minimization puts the purpose limit into practice.
Collect everything in case it's useful later
That's the opposite of purpose limitation.
Encrypt the data and collect as much as possible for future use
Encryption doesn't fix over-collection.
Ask users to promise they're adults
That's unrelated to purpose limitation.

q.q: While implementing a control, the team finds it can only partly meet the requirement this quarter. What should happen?
o: Document what's in place, record the gap in the POA&M with a date, and tell the system owner
Right. Partial implementation is visible and tracked, not hidden.
Report it as fully implemented
That misleads the AO.
Remove the control from the SSP
Removing it hides the requirement.
Wait until the audit and hope the assessor doesn't notice the gap
Hiding gaps destroys trust.

q.q: Why should controls be tested in a development or staging environment before going into production?
o: To catch problems before users see them
Right. Testing first reduces the chance a control causes an outage.
Because production controls never need testing once they're configured
Production controls are still assessed.
So the assessor can skip the assessment
Assessment still happens.
Because staging systems are more important
Production matters most. Staging protects it.

q.q: A cloud workload inherits encryption at rest from the provider. What should the system team still implement?
o: Its own part, like key access rules
Right. Inheritance covers the provider's part. Customer-configured parts remain the team's job.
Nothing, since inherited means the provider fully handles it
Many cloud controls are hybrid.
Its own data center locks
The provider handles physical security.
A new encryption algorithm
Creating your own crypto is a bad idea.

q.q: The system uses an AI model to rank benefit claims. Which control should the team implement to address AI risk in this setting?
o: Human review of high-impact decisions, plus monitoring of the model's results for bias and drift
Right. Oversight and monitoring catch harmful or drifting AI decisions.
Letting the model make every final decision with no review
High-impact decisions need human oversight.
Hiding the model's use from claimants
Transparency is part of responsible AI use.
Turning off all logging of model decisions
Logs are needed to review decisions.

q.q: For each control in the SSP, what should the implementation statement explain?
o: How it's met, by whom, with what evidence
Right. Clear statements let assessors verify the control quickly.
Only "Implemented"
A single word gives assessors nothing to check.
The vendor's marketing claims about the product's features
The SSP describes your implementation.
Why the control is annoying
Opinions don't belong in the SSP.

q.q: Which document tracks known weaknesses, the planned fixes, the resources needed and the due dates?
o: The plan of action and milestones (POA&M)
Right. The POA&M is how open weaknesses are tracked to closure.
The system security plan
The SSP describes controls, not the fix schedule.
The authorization decision letter
That records the AO's decision.
The rules of behavior
Rules of behavior tell users how to act.

q.q: A control is in place but leaves some residual risk the team can't remove yet. Where should that residual risk be recorded?
o: In the risk register or POA&M
Right. Leftover risk must be visible to decision makers.
Nowhere, since the control is already in place and working
Residual risk still needs tracking.
Only in an email to a coworker
Emails get lost and aren't part of the record.
In the user manual
User manuals aren't risk records.

q.q: Why should implementation documentation be kept current as the system changes?
o: Old documents mislead decision makers
Right. Decisions are only as good as the documents they're based on.
Documents are only read once, at the start of the project
They're used throughout the system's life.
Changes never affect controls
Changes often affect controls.
Auditors prefer old documents
Auditors expect documents to match reality.

q.q: An assessor asks for evidence that log reviews happen weekly. Which artifact is the BEST evidence?
o: Recent dated review records
Right. Records over time prove the activity really happens.
A sentence in the SSP that says reviews are done every week
That shows intent, not practice.
A screenshot of the log tool's login page
That proves nothing about reviews.
A promise from the ISSO
A promise isn't evidence.

q.q: What is the danger of copying another system's SSP text word for word?
o: It may not match this system
Right. Each SSP must describe its own system's implementation.
It makes the SSP too short
Length isn't the issue.
It's illegal to reuse any text
Reusing templates is fine. False details aren't.
Assessors can't accept any text that was copied from a template
They can read it. It just may be wrong.

q.q: Before an assessment starts, which document lays out its scope, methods, schedule, roles and deliverables?
o: The security assessment plan (SAP)
Right. The SAP is agreed before testing so everyone knows what will happen.
The security assessment report (SAR)
The SAR comes after testing.
The POA&M
The POA&M tracks fixes.
The incident report
Incident reports cover events.

q.q: Who should approve the assessment plan before testing begins?
o: The AO side, with the system owner
Right. Approval makes sure the assessment gives the AO what's needed for the decision.
The assessor alone
The assessor drafts it, but the AO side must agree.
Every end user
Users aren't approvers.
The hardware vendor whose servers will be tested
Vendors don't approve your assessment.

q.q: While preparing, the assessor finds a recent, valid assessment of the inherited common controls. What should she do?
o: Reuse the still-valid results
Right. Reusing valid results saves time without losing assurance.
Retest every inherited control from scratch to be completely sure
That duplicates work already done and accepted.
Ignore inherited controls completely
They still need to be accounted for.
Mark all inherited controls as failed
There's no basis for that.

q.q: Which preparation step helps avoid surprises during on-site testing?
o: Agreeing on rules of engagement
Right. Clear rules prevent outages and confusion during testing.
Starting scans without telling anyone
Surprise scans can cause outages and alarms.
Skipping the kickoff meeting to save time for testing
Kickoffs set expectations.
Only testing on weekends with no plan
Timing still needs a plan.

q.q: Which three assessment methods does NIST SP 800-53A describe?
o: Examine, interview and test
Right. Assessors review documents and settings, talk to people, and exercise controls.
Scan, patch and reboot
Those are operations tasks.
Plan, do and check
That's part of a general improvement cycle.
Detect, deter and delay
Those are physical security functions.

q.q: An assessor reads the access control policy and reviews firewall rule sets. Which method is she using?
o: Examine
Right. Examine means reviewing documents, records and configurations.
Interview
Interviewing means talking with people.
Test
Testing means exercising the control to see how it behaves.
Accept
Accepting is a risk response, not an assessment method.

q.q: An assessor tries to log in with a disabled account to confirm it really can't get in. Which method is this?
o: Test
Right. She is exercising the control under specific conditions.
Examine
She isn't reading documents. She's trying it.
Interview
She isn't asking anyone questions.
Tailor
Tailoring is part of control selection.

q.q: The admin says backups are tested monthly, but there's no record of any test. How should the assessor treat this?
o: Note that the claim isn't supported by evidence, so the control isn't shown to be in place
Right. Interviews must be backed by evidence.
Accept it, since the admin seems honest and experienced
Assessments rely on evidence, not trust.
Mark the control as not applicable
Backups clearly apply.
Fix the backups herself
Assessors report. They don't fix.

q.q: Why might an assessment include a penetration test in addition to reviewing settings?
o: To see if controls stop real attacks
Right. Pentests test how controls hold up against realistic attacks.
Because reviews of settings are never useful on their own
Reviews are useful. Pentests add depth.
To replace the SSP
A pentest doesn't document the system.
To fix vulnerabilities automatically
Pentests find and prove issues. They don't fix them.

q.q: Evidence for a control was collected 18 months ago. What should the assessor do?
o: Collect current evidence
Right. Evidence must be recent enough to reflect how the control works now.
Accept it, since evidence never expires
Systems change, so evidence ages.
Delete it from the file
Keep it for history, but get current evidence.
Mark the control as compliant without checking, since it passed before
That skips the assessment.

q.q: What should the initial assessment report include for each control that isn't fully met?
o: The finding, evidence and risk
Right. Findings must be traceable to evidence and explain the risk.
The name of the person to blame for each gap
Reports focus on controls and risk, not blame.
Only a pass or fail mark
A bare mark doesn't explain the risk.
A sales pitch for a fix
Assessors stay independent of products.

q.q: Why is the first version of the assessment report shared with the system owner before it's final?
o: To fix factual errors and start planning
Right. A draft review catches mistakes and starts remediation.
So the owner can delete any findings they disagree with
Owners can respond, but they can't remove valid findings.
So the report can be published online
Assessment reports are sensitive.
Because the AO never reads it
The AO relies on the final report.

q.q: An assessor finds a high-risk weakness that could be exploited now. What should she do before the report is final?
o: Alert the system owner right away
Right. Urgent risks shouldn't wait for paperwork.
Hide it until the final report
Waiting could let an attacker exploit it.
Exploit it to see how far she can get into the network
That goes beyond the agreed rules of engagement.
Tell other companies about it
Findings are confidential.

q.q: A finding has low risk, and fixing it would cost far more than the possible loss. Which risk response fits BEST?
o: Accept it, with AO sign-off
Right. Accepting is reasonable when the fix costs more than the risk.
Avoid it by shutting the whole system down
That's far too drastic for a low risk.
Ignore it and don't record anything
Accepted risk must still be documented.
Transfer it to the users
Users can't take on organizational risk.

q.q: After the system team fixes several findings, what should the assessor do?
o: Reassess those controls
Right. Fixes must be verified before findings are closed.
Close them based on the team's word
Closure needs verification.
Start a brand-new assessment of everything in the system
Only the fixed items need reassessment.
Leave them open forever
Verified fixes should be closed.

q.q: A company buys cyber insurance for a finding it can't fully fix this year. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer (share) the risk
Right. Insurance shifts part of the financial impact to another party.
Avoid the risk
The activity continues, so the risk isn't avoided.
Accept the risk
Buying insurance is an action, not acceptance.
Mitigate the risk
Insurance doesn't reduce the chance of the event.

q.q: Who should take part in deciding how to respond to each finding?
o: The owner, ISSO and AO side
Right. Responses balance mission, cost and risk, so key stakeholders must agree.
Only the assessor
Assessors advise. They don't own the response.
Only the newest team member, as a learning exercise
Decisions need the people accountable for the system.
The vendor's sales team
Vendors don't decide your risk responses.

q.q: In the final assessment report, what status can each control have?
o: Satisfied, other than satisfied, or N/A
Right. Each control gets a clear final status.
Pretty good, okay, needs work or bad
Reports use defined statuses, not opinions.
Green, yellow or purple
Colors aren't the defined statuses.
Draft, final or archived
Those describe documents, not controls.

q.q: Besides control status, what should the final report give the AO?
o: Recommendations and the remaining risk
Right. The AO needs a clear picture to make the authorization decision.
The assessor's opinion of each employee she interviewed
Personal opinions don't belong in the report.
A copy of every raw log file
Raw logs belong in the evidence, not the report body.
The authorization decision itself
The AO makes the decision, not the assessor.

q.q: Why should the final report be clear about which findings were fixed during the assessment?
o: So the AO sees the current risk
Right. The report should show the real state at the end.
So the system team gets a bonus
Bonuses aren't the reason.
Because fixed findings are always hidden from the final report
They're shown as resolved, not hidden.
So the assessment can be shorter
Clarity matters more than length.

q.q: After the final report, the team ranks remaining risks and estimates what each fix will take. What is it creating?
o: The risk response plan, which feeds the POA&M
Right. The plan ranks risks and estimates the resources needed to address them.
The incident response plan
IR plans handle incidents.
The system description
That was done in Scope.
The privacy notice
Privacy notices inform individuals.

q.q: Two open findings remain: one high risk and cheap to fix, one low risk and expensive. Which should the plan rank first?
o: The high-risk, cheap fix
Right. It removes the most risk for the least cost.
The low-risk, expensive fix
That spends more to remove less risk.
Whichever was found first
Discovery order doesn't decide priority.
Neither, until the next audit
Waiting leaves the high risk open.

q.q: Which set of documents usually makes up the authorization package for the AO?
o: The SSP, SAR and POA&M
Right. Together they show the system, what was found and how gaps will be fixed.
The user manual and the help desk FAQ
Those don't support a risk decision.
Only the vulnerability scan output
Scans are evidence, not the whole package.
The vendor contract and invoice
Contracts don't describe control status.

q.q: Before the package goes to the AO, the ISSO notices the SSP still lists a server that was retired. What should happen?
o: Correct the SSP first
Right. The AO must decide based on accurate documents.
Send it anyway, since one retired server doesn't matter
Inaccuracies undermine the whole decision.
Delete the SSP and send the rest
The SSP is required.
Add a note telling the AO to ignore errors
Fix the errors instead.

q.q: Why should the package include an executive summary?
o: The AO needs the key risks quickly
Right. Senior officials need the essentials up front.
To replace the detailed documents
The details still need to be there.
To list every log entry
That's raw evidence, not a summary.
To advertise the system to customers and partners
The package isn't marketing.

q.q: A privacy-relevant system's package is missing its privacy plan. What is the risk?
o: The AO and privacy official can't judge privacy risk, so the decision may be incomplete
Right. Privacy risk is part of the authorization decision.
No risk, since privacy plans are optional for most systems
Privacy requirements apply to systems that handle personal data.
The system will run slower
Documents don't affect speed.
Only the help desk is affected
The authorization decision is affected.

q.q: Why is it important to protect the authorization package itself?
o: It maps the system's weaknesses
Right. Packages are sensitive and should be shared only with those who need them.
It's too large to email
Size isn't the security reason.
It contains everyone's passwords
Passwords should never be in the package.
It must be printed and posted publicly for transparency
Packages aren't public.

q.q: Which document lets an AO decide quickly whether every finding has an owner and a due date?
o: The POA&M
Right. Each POA&M entry has an owner, milestones and dates.
The network diagram
Diagrams show architecture, not remediation.
The rules of behavior
Those are for users.
The hardware inventory
Inventories list assets.

q.q: The AO reviews the package and the residual risk. What is the residual risk compared against?
o: The organization's risk tolerance
Right. If residual risk is within tolerance, the AO can accept it.
The number of servers in the system
Size isn't the yardstick.
The vendor's market share
Market share doesn't measure your risk.
Last year's budget
Budget isn't the risk standard.

q.q: Which statement BEST describes residual risk at authorization?
o: The risk left after controls
Right. It's the risk the AO is being asked to accept.
The risk before any controls exist on the system
That's inherent risk.
Risk transferred to an insurer
Transferred risk is a treatment choice.
Risk that no longer matters
Residual risk still matters. It's just within tolerance.

q.q: An AO is unsure whether the residual risk is acceptable. Which action fits BEST?
o: Ask for more analysis or set conditions
Right. The AO can set conditions or ask for more information before deciding.
Approve it to avoid delays
Approving without confidence isn't responsible.
Let the system owner decide instead, since they know the system
The AO's responsibility can't be handed to the system owner.
Flip a coin
Decisions must be reasoned and documented.

q.q: Why should the accepted risks be written down clearly at authorization?
o: For accountability and later review
Right. Documented acceptance creates accountability and a basis for review.
So the assessor can be blamed later
Documentation is for accountability, not blame.
Because accepted risks disappear once they're written down
Writing them down doesn't remove the risk.
To make the package longer
Length isn't the goal.

q.q: A system depends on common controls whose provider has open high findings. How should this affect the system's risk posture?
o: The inherited weaknesses add to the system's residual risk
Right. The system shares the risk of the controls it inherits.
It has no effect, since the controls belong to someone else
Inheritance means shared risk.
It lowers the system's risk
Open findings raise risk.
It makes the system exempt from authorization
Nothing exempts the system.

q.q: Which factor should the AO weigh against the residual risk?
o: The system's mission importance
Right. Mission need is weighed against the risk of operating.
The SSP's font size
Formatting isn't a risk factor.
Which team has the newest laptops and monitors
That's irrelevant.
How many emails the ISSO sent
That doesn't measure risk.

q.q: The AO lets a system run for 12 months but requires two high findings to be fixed within 90 days. What decision is this?
o: An authorization to operate with conditions
Right. The system may run, with required actions and dates.
A denial of authorization
The system is allowed to run, so it isn't denied.
A common control authorization
That's for common control providers.
An interim test plan
This is an authorization decision, not a test plan.

q.q: An AO decides the residual risk is unacceptable and the system must not operate. What should happen next?
o: Document the denial, and the system doesn't run (or is stopped) until risks are reduced
Right. A denial means the system can't operate as is.
Run it anyway while appealing
A denial must be respected.
Rename the system and resubmit the same package next week
Renaming doesn't change the risk.
Ask users to vote on it
Authorization isn't a vote.

q.q: An agency wants to use another agency's authorized cloud service and accept its existing authorization evidence. What decision fits?
o: An authorization to use (ATU)
Right. An ATU lets an organization rely on another's authorization of a shared system or service.
A denial of authorization
Nothing is being denied.
A decommissioning order
The service is being adopted, not retired.
A security categorization
Categorization happens earlier.

q.q: Who must be told about the authorization decision?
o: The owner, ISSO and key stakeholders
Right. The decision and any conditions must reach those who act on them.
Only the AO's assistant
The people running the system need to know.
The general public
Decisions and packages are internal.
No one, since it's filed with the AO's records
Undisclosed decisions can't be followed.

q.q: What does the authorization decision document usually include besides approve or deny?
o: Conditions, terms and accepted risks
Right. Terms and conditions make the decision actionable.
The AO's vacation schedule
That's not part of the decision.
The full source code of the system for review
Code isn't part of the decision letter.
A list of user passwords
Passwords never belong in documents.

q.q: An agency uses ongoing authorization instead of a fixed three-year cycle. What makes this possible?
o: Mature continuous monitoring
Right. Ongoing authorization relies on timely monitoring data.
Skipping assessments altogether once the first ATO is signed
Controls are still assessed, often continuously.
Getting a new AO every month
The AO doesn't need to change.
Using only inherited controls
Inheritance alone doesn't enable it.

q.q: A team wants to add a new public API to an authorized system. What should happen BEFORE it goes live?
o: A security impact analysis, approval through change control, and updates to the SSP
Right. Changes are analyzed and approved, and documents are kept current.
Nothing, since the system is already authorized
Authorization covers the system as assessed, not unreviewed changes.
A brand-new full RMF cycle for every small change
Small changes go through change control, not a full restart.
Only a press release
Communication doesn't replace analysis.

q.q: A change significantly increases the system's risk, for example by moving it to a new cloud provider. What may this trigger?
o: Reassessment and possibly reauthorization
Right. Major changes can invalidate the basis of the original decision.
Nothing, if the old ATO hasn't expired
Significant changes need review regardless of the date.
Automatic decommissioning
The system can continue after review.
A new FIPS 199 for every user
Categorization is per system, not per user.

q.q: Why should every approved change have a rollback plan?
o: So a bad change can be undone
Right. Rollback limits damage from a bad change.
So changes never need testing
Testing is still needed.
To make the change ticket longer
Length isn't the purpose.
Because auditors like to see the word rollback in every ticket
It's about safety, not wording.

q.q: An admin made a firewall change with no ticket, and nothing broke. How should the ISSO treat it?
o: As an unauthorized change to investigate
Right. Untracked changes break the link between documents and reality.
As fine, since nothing broke
Unreviewed changes can create hidden risk.
As a reason to remove change control
One bypass shows why change control matters.
As a reason to delete the firewall logs so the record is clean
Logs are evidence. Keep them.

q.q: Which NIST publication guides building an information security continuous monitoring (ISCM) program?
o: Right. SP 800-137 covers ISCM strategy and programs.
SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
SP 800-60 covers mapping information types.
FIPS 197
FIPS 197 defines AES.

q.q: How often should each control be monitored under a continuous monitoring strategy?
o: Based on risk and how fast it changes
Right. Fast-changing or high-risk controls are checked more often.
Exactly once every three years for all controls
That's too slow for many controls.
Every control every minute
That's rarely practical or needed.
Only when an auditor asks
Monitoring should be ongoing, not on demand.

q.q: After a security incident, what should happen to the system's compliance documents?
o: Update them with what was learned
Right. Incidents often reveal control gaps that must be tracked.
Nothing, since incidents are separate from compliance work
Incidents directly affect risk and control status.
Delete the POA&M and start over
Existing tracking should be updated, not deleted.
Hide the incident from the AO
The AO needs to know about changes in risk.

q.q: Why should the contingency plan be tested and updated during operations?
o: An untested plan may fail when needed
Right. Regular tests keep recovery capability real.
Because contingency plans expire legally every month
There's no monthly legal expiry.
To give the help desk extra work
That isn't the reason.
Contingency plans never need changes
They need updates as the system changes.

q.q: A POA&M item is six months past its due date with no progress. What should the ISSO do?
o: Escalate it with a new plan
Right. Overdue risks need visibility and a decision.
Quietly change the due date so it no longer looks overdue
Hiding slippage misleads leadership.
Mark it as closed
It isn't fixed.
Delete it
Deleting removes the record of an open risk.

q.q: Which ongoing activity keeps users aware of their security duties after deployment?
o: Recurring training and rules of behavior
Right. Training and rules of behavior must continue during operations.
A one-time briefing at go-live only, with no follow-up
Awareness fades without repetition.
Sending the SSP to every user
Users need training, not the SSP.
Disabling user accounts every week
That disrupts work and doesn't build awareness.

q.q: An external auditor arrives for an annual review. What is the system team's main role?
o: Provide evidence and support the testing
Right. Supporting the audit openly gives an accurate result.
Limit the auditor to the parts of the system that look good
Steering the audit hides real risk.
Change settings during the audit to pass
Changes during an audit must go through change control and be disclosed.
Write the audit report for the auditor
The auditor writes the report.

q.q: Why keep evidence organized and mapped to each requirement throughout the year?
o: Faster audits and earlier gap spotting
Right. Continuous evidence collection reduces audit stress and surprises.
So auditors can skip testing
Auditors still test.
Evidence is only needed on the day the auditor arrives
Collecting it on the day is how gaps get missed.
It replaces the need for controls
Evidence shows controls work. It doesn't replace them.

q.q: An audit finds a control that was marked compliant last year now fails. What does this MOST likely show?
o: The control drifted since last year
Right. Controls can degrade, so monitoring must catch it between audits.
Last year's audit was illegal and must be thrown out
It may have been right at the time.
The control was never needed
A failing control still matters.
Audits should stop
Audits are exactly what found the problem.

q.q: A regulator requires an annual penetration test of the system. How should the team handle it?
o: Support it and track findings
Right. Required tests feed the same remediation process.
Skip it if last year's test came back clean
A required annual test must still happen.
Run it only on the test environment
The requirement usually covers production with safe rules.
Keep the findings secret from the AO
The AO needs to see the results.

q.q: A system is being retired. Which step protects the data on its storage?
o: Sanitize or destroy it per SP 800-88
Right. Media sanitization makes data unrecoverable, with proof.
Unplug the servers and leave them in storage
Stored drives still hold data.
Delete the files and reuse the drives elsewhere
Deleted files can often be recovered.
Give the drives to employees as gifts
That could expose sensitive data.

q.q: What should happen to the system's records, like the SSP and audit logs, when it's decommissioned?
o: Keep them for the retention period
Right. Records may be needed for audits, legal holds or investigations.
Delete them right away
They may need to be kept by law or policy.
Publish them online
They hold sensitive information.
Give them to the vendor that built the system
The organization keeps its own records.

q.q: Why should the AO and stakeholders agree to the decommissioning plan?
o: Others may depend on it or its data
Right. Agreement avoids breaking dependencies or losing data.
So the AO can delay the shutdown for as long as needed
Agreement is about doing it safely, not delaying it.
Because decommissioning needs a new ATO
Retiring doesn't need an ATO.
To decide who gets the old monitors
Furniture isn't the concern.

q.q: After decommissioning, which update keeps the organization's inventory and authorization records accurate?
o: Remove it from the inventory
Right. Accurate inventories stop old systems from looking active.
Leave it listed as active
That gives a false picture of risk.
Rename it to a test system and keep it listed
It's gone, not a test system.
Copy it to a new system ID
That creates a false record.

q.title: Match each task to its RMF step
q.scenario: Seven tasks from a new system's authorization. Pick the NIST RMF step each one belongs to.

rows.req: Set the organization's risk tolerance and name the common control providers.
rows.why: Organization-level setup happens in Prepare.

rows.req: Rate each information type's confidentiality, integrity and availability impact.
rows.why: FIPS 199 ratings are Categorize.

rows.req: Choose the moderate baseline and tailor it for the system.
rows.why: Picking and tailoring controls is Select.

rows.req: Configure audit logging and document how each control is met in the SSP.
rows.why: Putting controls in place is Implement.

rows.req: Examine, interview and test controls, then write the SAR.
rows.why: Evaluating controls is Assess.

rows.req: The AO reviews the package and signs an ATO with conditions.
rows.why: The risk decision is Authorize.

rows.req: Track changes, reassess key controls and report status every quarter.
rows.why: Ongoing checks are Monitor.

q.title: Set each system's impact level
q.scenario: Four systems and the highest ratings across their information types. Use the high-water mark to pick each system's overall impact level.

rows.req: Public website: C Low, I Moderate, A Low.
rows.why: The highest rating, integrity, is Moderate.

rows.req: Cafeteria menu app: C Low, I Low, A Low.
rows.why: Every objective is Low.

rows.req: Law enforcement case system: C High, I Moderate, A Moderate.
rows.why: Confidentiality is High, so the system is High.

rows.req: Payroll system: C Moderate, I Moderate, A Low.
rows.why: The highest rating is Moderate.

q.title: Match each document to its purpose
q.scenario: Five documents an AO might see. Pick what each one is for. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Describes the system, its boundary and how each control is implemented.
items.why: The system security plan describes the system and its controls.

items.text: Records the assessor's findings and each control's status.
items.why: The security assessment report holds the assessment results.

items.text: Lists open weaknesses with owners, milestones and due dates.
items.why: The plan of action and milestones tracks remediation.

items.text: Documents the security terms of a connection between two systems.
items.why: An interconnection security agreement covers system-to-system links.

items.text: Analyzes how the system collects, uses and protects personal data.
items.why: A privacy impact assessment covers privacy risk.

q.title: Choose a response for each finding
q.scenario: Five findings after an assessment. Pick the risk response that fits each situation best.

rows.req: A low-risk banner wording issue that would cost more to fix than any likely harm. The AO signs off.
rows.why: Low risk and high cost to fix fits documented acceptance.

rows.req: An unneeded public file-sharing feature creates high risk. The team removes the feature.
rows.why: Removing the risky activity avoids the risk.

rows.req: Missing MFA on admin accounts. The team turns on MFA within 30 days.
rows.why: Adding a control reduces the risk.

rows.req: Breach costs could be large. The organization buys cyber insurance.
rows.why: Insurance shares the financial impact with another party.

rows.req: Unpatched web server. The team patches it and verifies the fix.
rows.why: Patching is a control that reduces the risk.

q.title: Who does what in authorization
q.scenario: Five responsibilities. Pick the role that owns each one. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Formally accepts the risk of operating the system.
items.why: The AO makes the authorization decision.

items.text: Accountable for the system's development, operation and SSP.
items.why: The system owner is accountable for the system.

items.text: Handles day-to-day security and keeps the SSP and POA&M current.
items.why: The ISSO runs daily security work.

items.text: Independently examines, interviews and tests the controls.
Oversees privacy risk across the organization.
items.why: The senior agency official for privacy owns privacy risk.

q.title: Pick the assessment method
q.scenario: Five assessor activities. Pick the SP 800-53A method each one uses.

rows.req: Read the incident response plan and last quarter's incident tickets.
